# What is a definition of the trace norm? I have found that (one?) definition of the trace norm is. > In particular, we will restrict the trace norm of the (driving) Hamiltonian $\| H\_t \| < E\_{\mathrm{max}}$. Is the trace norm here defined as in Eq.(1)? * $\begingroup$ @NorbertSchuch My understanding is that the trace norm is the sum of singular values while the operator norm is the maximum of singular values. Why exactly do we bound the Hamiltonian by the operator norm? ## 2 Answers 2. The trace norm $\|H\|$ of a matrix H is the sum of all the singular values of H. The singular values are the roots of the eigenvalues of $HH^\dagger$. For a Hermitian matrix, like in our case Hamiltonian matrix, the singular values are the absolute value of eigenvalues. So the trace norm is just the sum of the absolute value of the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian matrix at a particular time. answered Feb 3, 2019 at 14:01. The trace norm is just the sum of the singular values. To see how this works, consider the singular value decomposition: $$A=U\Sigma V^\dagger.$$ Here $U,V$ are unitary matrices and $\Sigma$ is a diagonal matrix and $\dagger$ is the complex conjugate. The values on the diagonal of $\Sigma$ are called the *singular values* of $A$. The singular values are unique, but $U$ and $V$ are not: you can find multiple $U$'s and $V$'s for a single matrix. Now consider $A^\dagger A$: \begin{align} A^\dagger A&=(V\Sigma^\*U^\dagger)(U\Sigma V^\dagger)\\ &=V\Sigma^\*\Sigma V^\dagger\\ &=V|\Sigma|^2 V^\dagger \end{align} The matrix $|\Sigma|^2$ is a diagonal matrix with the absolute value squared of the singular values along its diagonal. \end{align} From this fact we can reason that any function that is expressable as a power series can be applied to $A^\dagger A$ by applying it to $|\Sigma|^2$. So taking the square root of this expression we get $$\sqrt{A^\dagger A}=V|\Sigma|V^\dagger$$ Finally, the trace norm is just the sum of the absolute values of the singular values:. $$\text{tr}\sqrt{A^\dagger A}=\text{tr}|\Sigma|=\sum\_i|\Sigma\_{ii}|$$. Let $A,B$ be $n\times n $ matrices and denote by $A\star B$ the Hadamard product $(A\star B)(i,j)=A(i,j)B(i,j)$ (pointwise matrix multiplication). My question is what happens if we drop the positive definiteness assumption, i.e. what is the best constant $C>0$ such that. $$\|A\star B\| \leq C \sup\_{i,j} |A(i,j)| \|B\|$$. First, let me prove that $C=\sqrt{n}$ works. Thus $$\|(A\star B)v\|\leq\sum|v\_i|\|(A\star B)e\_i\|\leq a\|B\|\sum|v\_i|.$$ By Cauchy-Schwarz, $\sum|v\_i|\leq \sqrt{n}\|v\|$, so we conclude that $\|A\star B\|\leq a\|B\|\sqrt{n}$ and $C=\sqrt{n}$ works. To prove $C=\sqrt{n}$ is optimal, let $\omega$ be a primitive $n$th root of unity and let $B(i,j)=\frac{\omega^{ij}}{\sqrt{n}}$. Now let $A(i,j)=\omega^{-ij}$, so that $A\star B$ is the matrix whose entries are all $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$. We have $\|A\star B\|=\sqrt{n}$ (the vector of all $1$s is an eigenvector of $A\star B$ with eigenvalue $\sqrt{n}$). Since $|A(i,j)|=1$ for all $i,j$, this means we must have $C\geq \sqrt{n}$.
